clinicalPearls: 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency is the second most common form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia and results from autosomal recessive loss-of-function variants in CYP11B1
The enzyme block impairs conversion of 11-deoxycortisol to cortisol and of 11-deoxycorticosterone to corticosterone, so cortisol falls and precursors accumulate

Loss of cortisol negative feedback drives ACTH, shunting steroid production into the androgen pathway and causing virilisation, with ambiguous genitalia in affected girls and precocious virilisation in boys
Unlike the common 21-hydroxylase form, this variant characteristically causes hypertension rather than salt wasting, because the accumulating 11-deoxycorticosterone has mineralocorticoid activity
The hypertension is typically low-renin and may be accompanied by hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis
Diagnosis rests on demonstrating raised 11-deoxycortisol and 11-deoxycorticosterone (and their metabolites) with elevated adrenal androgens
Treatment is glucocorticoid replacement to suppress excess ACTH and adrenal androgen production, which also controls the mineralocorticoid-driven hypertension
reference.pathophysiology: 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency is an autosomal recessive disorder of adrenal steroidogenesis caused by variants in CYP11B1, which encodes the enzyme catalysing the final step of cortisol synthesis in the zona fasciculata. Because cortisol cannot be produced efficiently, the loss of negative feedback increases pituitary ACTH secretion, driving adrenal hyperplasia and diverting accumulated precursors down the androgen pathway; the resulting androgen excess produces virilisation, presenting as ambiguous genitalia in genetic females and early virilisation in males. At the same time, the enzyme block causes accumulation of 11-deoxycorticosterone, a steroid with intrinsic mineralocorticoid activity, which drives sodium retention and volume-dependent, low-renin hypertension often accompanied by hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis. This mineralocorticoid excess distinguishes the condition from the salt-wasting 21-hydroxylase form.
additionalDifferentials: 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency (hypertension but with hypogonadism rather than virilisation)
Other causes of disorders of sex development / ambiguous genitalia
Other secondary hypertension in the young
additionalInvestigations: Adrenal steroid profile showing raised 11-deoxycortisol and 11-deoxycorticosterone
Serum androgens (e.g. androstenedione, testosterone) and ACTH
Serum electrolytes for hypokalaemic alkalosis and blood pressure assessment
Karyotype and pelvic imaging in ambiguous genitalia
redFlags: Severe hypertension with end-organ effects in a child
Ambiguous genitalia requiring urgent multidisciplinary assessment
Rapid virilisation and accelerated bone maturation
Adrenal crisis during intercurrent illness or under-replacement
reference.prognosis: With glucocorticoid replacement to control ACTH-driven androgen and precursor overproduction, virilisation and hypertension can be managed and growth optimised, though long-standing or poorly controlled disease may leave residual hypertension and its cardiovascular consequences.
pitfalls: Assuming all congenital adrenal hyperplasia causes salt wasting and missing the hypertensive presentation
Overlooking the mineralocorticoid effect of accumulated 11-deoxycorticosterone as the cause of low-renin hypertension
Attributing the hypertension to primary hyperaldosteronism despite suppressed aldosterone
Under- or over-replacing glucocorticoid, risking either androgen excess or iatrogenic Cushingoid effects
Failing to arrange sensitive multidisciplinary care for ambiguous genitalia
references: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline on congenital adrenal hyperplasia
management: Give glucocorticoid replacement, typically hydrocortisone in children, to restore cortisol and suppress ACTH-driven androgen and precursor overproduction.
Increase glucocorticoid cover during intercurrent illness, injury or surgery, and treat adrenal crisis with parenteral hydrocortisone and fluids.
Control the mineralocorticoid-excess hypertension, adding a mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonist or other antihypertensive if glucocorticoid alone is insufficient, and correct hypokalaemia.
Monitor growth, bone age, blood pressure, potassium and adrenal androgen levels to titrate therapy.
Manage atypical genitalia through a specialist disorders-of-sex-development multidisciplinary team, with surgical and psychological input.
Provide genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance, with CYP11B1 testing and family screening.
Coordinate long-term paediatric and adult endocrinology follow-up, addressing fertility and cardiovascular risk.
